title: The Information Sharing Behaviors of Dietitians and Twitter Users in the Nutrition and COVID-19 Infodemic: Content Analysis Study of Tweets
screen_reason: Content analysis of 2,886 nutrition-and-COVID-19 tweets in which every evaluable tweet was compared against expert nutrition recommendations and coded accurate / inaccurate / not applicable, with counts and denominators given separately for dietitians (532/575, 92.5% accurate) and the public (250/382, 65.5% accurate). Guideline concordance stated as accurate/inaccurate is CONTENT under the governing rule.

estimates.country: Not restricted (English-language public Twitter users worldwide; country of origin collected only where available and not used to filter)
estimates.date: Tweets published 31 December 2019 to 31 December 2020 (accuracy coding carried out April-July 2021)
estimates.measure_type: % of general-public nutrition/COVID-19 tweets evaluable for accuracy that were coded inaccurate against expert nutrition recommendations
estimates.denominator: 382 public tweets for which accuracy could be evaluated (of 1,469 analysed public tweets; the other 1,087, 74.0%, were 'not applicable' for accuracy)
estimates.definition: Coders read the tweet and verified its information against one or more reliable recommendations pertaining to its specific content; if the content was in line with the recommendation it was deemed accurate, and 'if the content differed from the recommendation in any way, it was deemed inaccurate'. Recipes/meal ideas, questions, reports of study results and non-scientific declarations or opinions were coded 'not applicable' and excluded from the denominator.
estimates.misinfo_def: "False information includes both misinformation and disinformation. Although the former is unintentional, the latter is done deliberately, in order to cause harm"; operationalised as tweet content that differs from evidence-based nutrition and food-related recommendations regarding COVID-19.
estimates.source_quote: A higher proportion of dietitians’ tweets were accurate compared with the public’s tweets (532/575, 92.5% vs 250/382, 65.5%; P<.001).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Research Question #3: Content Accuracy' (p. 10); Table 7; Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two team members (EC and LJC) compared each tweet against a purpose-built database of recommendations from reliable expert sources (Dietitians of Canada, Health Canada, Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics), supplemented for specific content by PubMed and Mayo Clinic. Two rounds of reliability coding; Cohen kappa for content accuracy = 0.67 in the public group and 0.78 in the dietitian group (Table 2). The authors note that coding ran April-July 2021 against the recommendations current at that time.
estimates.moderator_quote: To determine tweets' content accuracy and thus reveal the presence of misinformation, 2 team members (EC and LJC) compared the 2886 tweets against evidence-based nutrition and food-related recommendations regarding COVID-19. ... If its content was in line with the recommendation, it was deemed accurate. If the content differed from the recommendation in any way, it was deemed inaccurate. Thus, tweets were categorized as accurate, inaccurate, or not applicable.
estimates.notes: VALUE DERIVATION - the authors print only the ACCURACY share (250/382, 65.5%); the inaccurate share entered here is the exact count complement inside the same verbatim denominator (382-250 = 132; 132/382 = 34.55%). It is consistent with Table 7, whose columns are headed 'Accurate (N=782)' and 'Inaccurate (N=175)' and whose totals reconcile exactly (532+250=782; 43+132=175). A strict reading of R8 ('never keep a complement you computed') would keep only the 65.5% accuracy figure; flagged here so the adjudicator can choose. MAJOR DENOMINATOR CAVEAT: accuracy was evaluable for only 382 of 1,469 public tweets (1,087, 74.0%, were 'not applicable' - recipes, questions, study reports, opinions), so this share is over a strongly selected evaluable subset and is NOT the share of all public nutrition/COVID tweets that were inaccurate. Breadth coded misleading because 'differed from the recommendation in any way' is a broad, guideline-concordance criterion rather than strict falsity. Country=Global: only the dietitian sample was restricted to Canada and the US; the public sample was English-language tweets with no country filter.

estimates.country: Canada and the United States (registered dietitians identified from Dietitians of Canada and Nutrition Blog Network directories)
estimates.date: Tweets published 31 December 2019 to 31 December 2020 (accuracy coding carried out April-July 2021)
estimates.measure_type: % of registered dietitians' nutrition/COVID-19 tweets evaluable for accuracy that were coded inaccurate against expert nutrition recommendations
estimates.denominator: 575 dietitian tweets for which accuracy could be evaluated (of 1,417 analysed dietitian tweets; the other 842, 59.4%, were 'not applicable' for accuracy)
estimates.definition: Identical coding rule to the public row: tweet content compared with reliable COVID-19 nutrition recommendations; in line = accurate, differing in any way = inaccurate; recipes, questions, study reports and opinions = not applicable.
estimates.misinfo_def: "False information includes both misinformation and disinformation. Although the former is unintentional, the latter is done deliberately, in order to cause harm"; operationalised as tweet content that differs from evidence-based nutrition and food-related recommendations regarding COVID-19.
estimates.source_quote: A higher proportion of dietitians’ tweets were accurate compared with the public’s tweets (532/575, 92.5% vs 250/382, 65.5%; P<.001).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Research Question #3: Content Accuracy' (p. 10); Table 7; Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same procedure and coders as the public row; kappa for content accuracy in the dietitian group = 0.78 (Table 2).
estimates.moderator_quote: In order to identify our sample of RDs from Canada and the United States with Twitter accounts, the Dietitians of Canada Member Blogs list [35] (n=56 as of October 2020) and the American Nutrition Blog Network author directory [36] (n=1049 as of October 2020) were used. ... The final list thus comprised a total of 625 Twitter accounts.
estimates.notes: Same derivation caveat as the public row: 92.5% accurate is verbatim, 7.5% inaccurate is its exact count complement within the verbatim 575 denominator (575-532 = 43). Same evaluable-subset caveat (only 575 of 1,417 dietitian tweets could be scored; 842, 59.4%, not applicable). This row is a professional/elite-source comparison group, not a general-population prevalence: the accounts come from a curated list of 625 registered dietitians built from two blog directories, hence denom_selection=curated and sampling_frame=curated_seed. The authors themselves flag that some health professionals may have fallen into the public sample.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) 'out of 73,323 English-language tweets published by dietitians during the 1-year period, only 1417 (1.9%) pertained to COVID-19 and nutrition' - topical relevance of dietitians' output, not a falsity share; (2) the 'not applicable' shares (dietitians 842/1417, 59.4%; public 1087/1469, 74.0%) and their four reasons (recipe/meal idea 332/1087, 30.5% vs 205/842, 24.4%; study results 118/842, 14.0% vs 8/1087, 0.7%; opinions 806/1087, 74.2% vs 551/842, 65.4%) - unevaluable-content shares, recorded here because they define how selective the accuracy denominators are; (3) Table 7's per-theme columns, which distribute the 782 accurate and 175 inaccurate tweets ACROSS themes (e.g. immune health 77/175, 44.0% of all inaccurate tweets; weight loss 30/175, 17.1%) - these are shares of the inaccurate pool, not the inaccuracy rate within a theme, and the two groups are pooled, so no per-theme prevalence can be recovered without recomputation; (4) an overall pooled inaccuracy rate (175 inaccurate of 782+175 = 957 evaluable, 18.3%) - not extracted because 957 is a cross-category sum I would have to compute, which R8 forbids; (5) all theme frequencies (Table 3), TDF domain frequencies (Table 8-9) and engagement means (Tables 4-6) - not falsity measures. Judgement call for the adjudicator: this study reports ACCURACY, never inaccuracy, so both extracted values are count complements inside verbatim denominators; and both denominators are the small 'evaluable' subsets, so the numbers are not comparable to studies that classify a whole corpus.

rob.design: Retrospective content analysis of public English-language tweets, 31 Dec 2019 - 31 Dec 2020, collected via the Twitter Premium API. Two frames: (a) a curated list of 625 registered-dietitian accounts built from the Dietitians of Canada Member Blogs list (n=56) and the American Nutrition Blog Network author directory (n=1,049), minus 16 suspended/private accounts; (b) general public tweets matching a list of nutrition and COVID-19 hashtags/keywords (initially 2,561 COVID + 41 nutrition + 16 combined terms, later refined with 350 more specific terms). 6,670 public and 4,627 dietitian tweets at step 1; 4,210 after refiltering (RDs 1,914; public 2,296); 2,886 finally analysed (RDs 1,417; public 1,469) after dropping tweets not about both nutrition and COVID-19. Coding procedure: inductive 15-theme codebook, deductive TDF coding, and accuracy coding against a database of expert recommendations, by two coders (EC, LJC) with disagreements settled by a third author (SD). Reliability as reported (Table 2, after two rounds): COVID/nutrition relevance kappa 0.78 public / 0.95 dietitian; content accuracy 0.67 public / 0.78 dietitian; themes 0.54 then 0.65 (public) and 0.51 then 0.79 (dietitian); TDF domains 0.42 then 0.63 (public) and 0.66 then 0.75 (dietitian). No response rate applicable (platform data). Ethics review waived (public content). Author-declared limitations: non-specific keywords, non-representative RD list, possible dietitians inside the public sample.
rob.item6_quote: First, a database of recommendations from reliable and expert sources that covered COVID-19 and nutrition-related themes, such as Dietitians of Canada, Health Canada, and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, was elaborated through web searches. ... Second, during coding, coders read the tweet and verified its information using one or many reliable recommendations pertaining to the specific content of that tweet. If its content was in line with the recommendation, it was deemed accurate. If the content differed from the recommendation in any way, it was deemed inaccurate. Thus, tweets were categorized as accurate, inaccurate, or not applicable.
rob.item10_quote: For dietitians, out of a total of 575 tweets for which accuracy could be evaluated, 532 (92.5%) were accurate. As for the public, out of 382 tweets, 250 (65.5%) were accurate.
